claim: Patients with APAP-induced liver failure display higher levels of Chi3l1 in the liver compared with healthy individuals.
source: Our data demonstrated, for the first time, that compared with healthy individuals, patients with AILI displayed higher levels of Chi3l1 in the liver and serum (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1A comparing normal liver biopsies with patient samples.

claim: Patients with APAP-induced liver failure display higher levels of Chi3l1 in serum compared with healthy individuals.
source: Our data demonstrated, for the first time, that compared with healthy individuals, patients with AILI displayed higher levels of Chi3l1 in the liver and serum (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA analysis data shown in Figure 1B comparing serum from healthy individuals (n=6) with patients with AILI (n=29).

claim: In mice treated with APAP, hepatic mRNA levels of Chi3l1 were upregulated.
source: Similarly, in mice treated with APAP, hepatic mRNA and serum protein levels of Chi3l1 were upregulated (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C measuring Chil1 mRNA in liver homogenates at 3 and 24 hr after APAP treatment.

claim: In mice treated with APAP, serum protein levels of Chi3l1 were upregulated.
source: Similarly, in mice treated with APAP, hepatic mRNA and serum protein levels of Chi3l1 were upregulated (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D measuring Chi3l1 protein levels in serum at 3 and 24 hr after APAP treatment.

claim: Chil1-/- mice develop dramatically lower serum ALT levels compared with WT mice after APAP treatment.
source: Compared with WT mice, serum ALT levels and the extent of liver necrosis were dramatically lower in Chil1-/- mice (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT measurement data shown in Figure 1E at 24 hr after APAP treatment.

claim: Chil1-/- mice develop dramatically lower extent of liver necrosis compared with WT mice after APAP treatment.
source: Compared with WT mice, serum ALT levels and the extent of liver necrosis were dramatically lower in Chil1-/- mice (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by liver histology data shown in Figure 1F at 24 hr after APAP treatment.

claim: Administration of rmChi3l1 protein to Chil1-/- mice enhanced liver injury to a similar degree observed in APAP-treated WT mice.
source: Moreover, administration of rmChi3l1 protein to Chil1-/- mice enhanced liver injury to a similar degree observed in APAP-treated WT mice (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 1E,F comparing Chil1-/- mice treated with PBS versus rmChi3l1.

claim: Chi3l1 contributes to AILI.
source: These data strongly suggest that Chi3l1 contributes to AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Chil1-/- mice have reduced liver injury and that rmChi3l1 administration restores injury.

claim: Thrombocytopenia is often observed in patients with APAP overdose.
source: Thrombocytopenia is often observed in patients with APAP overdose (Harrison et al., 1990; Stravitz et al., 2013; Stravitz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Patients with APAP-induced liver failure have markedly increased numbers of platelets in the liver compared with normal liver tissues.
source: We performed IHC staining of liver biopsies from patients with APAP-induced liver failure and found markedly increased numbers of platelets compared with normal liver tissues (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 2A detecting CD41+ platelets in patient liver biopsies versus normal controls.

claim: In mice treated with APAP, a marked increase of platelets in the liver was observed.
source: Similarly, in mice treated with APAP, a marked increase of platelets in the liver was observed by intravital microscopy (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 2B comparing PBS versus APAP treatment.

claim: Depletion of platelets prior to APAP treatment can prevent liver injury in mice.
source: It is reported that depletion of platelets prior to APAP treatment can prevent liver injury in mice (Miyakawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Even after APAP treatment, depletion of platelets could still attenuate AILI.
source: Our data demonstrated that even after APAP treatment, depletion of platelets could still attenuate AILI (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 2C,D comparing control IgG versus anti-CD41 antibody treatment administered 3 hr after APAP.

claim: Platelets critically contribute to AILI.
source: These data indicate a critical contribution of platelets to AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that platelet depletion attenuates liver injury.

claim: Chi3l1 plays a role in promoting intrahepatic coagulation in concanavalin A-induced hepatitis.
source: Given the role of Chi3l1 in promoting intrahepatic coagulation in concanavalin A-induced hepatitis (Shan et al., 2018), we hypothesized that Chi3l1 might be involved in platelet recruitment to the liver during AILI.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by the authors.

claim: Chil1-/- mice have much fewer platelets in the liver after APAP treatment compared to WT mice.
source: Comparing with WT mice, we observed much fewer platelets in the liver after APAP treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2E detecting CD41+ platelets in WT versus Chil1-/- mice.

claim: Administration of rmChi3l1 to Chil1-/- mice restored hepatic platelet accumulation similar to APAP-treated WT mice.
source: Moreover, administration of rmChi3l1 to Chil1-/- mice restored hepatic platelet accumulation similar to APAP-treated WT mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2E comparing Chil1-/- mice treated with PBS versus rmChi3l1.

claim: Chi3l1 plays a critical role in promoting hepatic platelet accumulation, thereby contributing to AILI.
source: These data suggest that Chi3l1 plays a critical role in promoting hepatic platelet accumulation, thereby contributing to AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Chil1-/- mice have reduced platelet accumulation and liver injury, and that rmChi3l1 restores both.

claim: The anti-CD44 antibody could 'pull down' Chi3l1 from WT but not Cd44-/- liver homogenates.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments using liver homogenates from APAP-treated WT and Cd44-/- mice demonstrated that the anti-CD44 antibody could 'pull down' Chi3l1 from WT but not Cd44-/- liver homogenates (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a direct interaction between Chi3l1 and CD44 with Kd = 251 nM.
source: Supporting this finding, interferometry measurements using rhChi3l1 revealed a direct interaction between Chi3l1 and CD44 (Kd = 251 nM, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by bio-layer interferometry data shown in Figure 3B measuring binding kinetics between His-Chi3l1 and Fc-CD44.

claim: Chi3l1 directly binds to CD44.
source: Data shown in Figure 3C confirmed that Chi3l1 directly binds to CD44.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C where His-tagged Chi3l1 was incubated with recombinant CD44.

claim: CD44 is a receptor for Chi3l1.
source: Together, these results suggest that CD44 is a receptor for Chi3l1.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing direct binding between Chi3l1 and CD44.

claim: rmChi3l1 had no effect on platelet recruitment in Cd44-/- mice.
source: We found that rmChi3l1 had no effect on platelet recruitment or AILI in Cd44-/- mice (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3F comparing Cd44-/- mice treated with PBS versus rmChi3l1.

claim: rmChi3l1 had no effect on AILI in Cd44-/- mice.
source: We found that rmChi3l1 had no effect on platelet recruitment or AILI in Cd44-/- mice (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 3D,E comparing Cd44-/- mice treated with PBS versus rmChi3l1.

claim: The effects of rmChi3l1 in Chil1-/- mice were abrogated when CD44 was blocked by using an anti-CD44 antibody.
source: However, these effects of rmChi3l1 in Chil1-/- mice were abrogated when CD44 was blocked by using an anti-CD44 antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT, liver histology, and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: CD44 plays a critical role in mediating Chi3l1-induced hepatic platelet accumulation and AILI.
source: Together, these data demonstrate a critical role of CD44 in mediating Chi3l1-induced hepatic platelet accumulation and AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that rmChi3l1 cannot restore platelet accumulation or liver injury in Cd44-/- mice or when CD44 is blocked.

claim: Chi3l1 or CD44 deletion does not affect APAP bio-activation and its direct toxicity to hepatocytes.
source: However, we did not observe any difference, suggesting that Chi3l1 or CD44 deletion does not affect APAP bio-activation and its direct toxicity to hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C comparing GSH levels, CYP2E1 expression, and NAPQI-protein adducts among WT, Chil1-/-, and Cd44-/- mice.

claim: Female Chil1-/- and Cd44-/- mice show a similar phenotype as male mice in AILI.
source: Moreover, although we used male mice performed all of the experiments, we observed a similar phenotype in female Chil1-/- and Cd44-/- mice as in male mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 comparing female WT, Chil1-/-, and Cd44-/- mice.

claim: Almost all CD44+Chi3l1+ cells were F4/80+ macrophages.
source: We found that almost all CD44+Chi3l1+ cells were F4/80+ Mɸs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D identifying Chi3l1-binding cells among liver NPCs.

claim: Co-localization of macrophages (CD68+) and platelets (CD41+) was observed in liver biopsies from AILI patients.
source: We performed IHC staining of liver biopsies from AILI patients and observed co-localization of Mɸs (CD68+) and platelets (CD41+) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the livers of APAP-treated mice, adherence of platelets to macrophages was observed.
source: In the livers of APAP-treated mice, adherence of platelets to Mɸs was also observed by IHC (Figure 4B) and intravital microscopy (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4B and intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were higher numbers of platelets adherent to macrophages than to liver sinusoidal endothelial cells after APAP challenge.
source: Quantification of the staining confirmed that there were higher numbers of platelets adherent to Mɸs than to liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) after APAP challenge (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B comparing platelets adherent to KCs versus LSECs.

claim: Using the 'Previous Strategy' of CLDN treatment (40 hr prior to APAP), there were more macrophages, consisting mainly of infiltrating macrophages, in the liver of CLDN-treated mice compared with control mice.
source: We found that compared with control mice treated with empty liposomes, there were actually more Mɸs, consisted of mainly IMs, in the liver of CLDN-treated mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C comparing PBS versus CLDN treatment using the 'Previous Strategy'.

claim: Using the 'Previous Strategy' of CLDN treatment, there were higher numbers of platelets in the liver of CLDN-treated mice.
source: Consistent with the increase of Mɸs, there were also higher numbers of platelets in the liver of CLDN-treated mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4C comparing PBS versus CLDN treatment using the 'Previous Strategy'.

claim: Using the 'Previous Strategy' of CLDN treatment resulted in exacerbated AILI.
source: As reported, this treatment strategy resulted in exacerbated AILI (Figure 4E,F, 'Previous Strategy'), which had led to the conclusion in published reports that KCs play a protective role against AILI (Campion et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2013; Ju et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 4E,F comparing PBS versus CLDN treatment using the 'Previous Strategy'.

claim: Using the 'New Strategy' of CLDN treatment (9 hr prior to APAP), both KCs and IMs were dramatically reduced at 6 hr after APAP challenge.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, at 6 hr after APAP challenge (15 hr after CLDN), both KCs and IMs were dramatically reduced.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D comparing PBS versus CLDN treatment using the 'New Strategy'.

claim: Using the 'New Strategy' of CLDN treatment, CLDN-treated mice developed markedly reduced liver injury with nearly no platelet accumulation in the liver compared to control mice.
source: Interestingly, when compared to control mice treated with empty liposomes, CLDN-treated mice developed markedly reduced liver injury with nearly no platelet accumulation in the liver (Figure 4D–F, 'New Strategy').
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence, serum ALT, and liver histology data shown in Figure 4D–F comparing PBS versus CLDN treatment using the 'New Strategy'.

claim: Hepatic macrophages play a crucial role in platelet recruitment into the liver, thereby contributing to AILI.
source: These data suggest that hepatic Mɸs play a crucial role in platelet recruitment into the liver, thereby contributing to AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that depletion of hepatic macrophages reduces platelet accumulation and liver injury.

claim: Podoplanin is expressed at a much higher level in hepatic macrophages isolated from APAP-treated WT mice than those from Chil1-/- or Cd44-/- mice.
source: Our data showed that podoplanin is expressed at a much higher level in hepatic Mɸs isolated from APAP-treated WT mice than those from Chil1-/- or Cd44-/- mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A measuring mRNA levels of various adhesion molecules in macrophages.

claim: rmChi3l1 treatment of Chil1-/-, but not Cd44-/- mice, markedly increased the podoplanin mRNA expression levels in macrophages.
source: Interestingly, rmChi3l1 treatment of Chil1-/-, but not Cd44-/- mice, markedly increased the podoplanin mRNA and protein expression levels in Mɸs (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B measuring Pdpn mRNA levels in macrophages.

claim: rmChi3l1 treatment of Chil1-/-, but not Cd44-/- mice, markedly increased the podoplanin protein expression levels in macrophages.
source: Interestingly, rmChi3l1 treatment of Chil1-/-, but not Cd44-/- mice, markedly increased the podoplanin mRNA and protein expression levels in Mɸs (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 5C detecting podoplanin and F4/80.

claim: Blockade of podoplanin abrogated rmChi3l1-mediated platelet recruitment into the liver in Chil1-/- mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5D–F, blockade of podoplanin not only abrogated rmChi3l1-mediated platelet recruitment into the liver but also significantly reduced its effect on increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 5F comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-podoplanin Ab treatment.

claim: Blockade of podoplanin significantly reduced rmChi3l1's effect on increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5D–F, blockade of podoplanin not only abrogated rmChi3l1-mediated platelet recruitment into the liver but also significantly reduced its effect on increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 5D,E comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-podoplanin Ab treatment.

claim: Clec-2 is the only platelet receptor known to bind podoplanin.
source: Clec-2 is the only platelet receptor known to bind podoplanin (Kerrigan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Clec-2-expressing platelets only bound to IgG-treated, but not anti-podoplanin-treated macrophages.
source: IF staining of podoplanin and Clec-2 showed that the Clec-2-expressing platelets only bound to IgG-treated, but not anti-podoplanin-treated Mɸs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Macrophages recruit platelets through podoplanin and Clec-2 interaction.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that Mɸs recruit platelets through podoplanin and Clec-2 interaction, and that the podoplanin expression on Mɸs is regulated by Chi3l1/CD44 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing podoplanin expression is regulated by Chi3l1/CD44 and that blocking podoplanin prevents platelet recruitment.

claim: The podoplanin expression on macrophages is regulated by Chi3l1/CD44 signaling.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that Mɸs recruit platelets through podoplanin and Clec-2 interaction, and that the podoplanin expression on Mɸs is regulated by Chi3l1/CD44 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that podoplanin expression is higher in WT than Chil1-/- or Cd44-/- mice, and that rmChi3l1 increases podoplanin in Chil1-/- but not Cd44-/- mice.

claim: The death rate and need for liver transplantation from APAP overdose remain unacceptably high despite NAC treatment.
source: Although NAC greatly reduces morbidity and mortality from ALF due to APAP overdose, the death rate and need for liver transplantation remain unacceptably high.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical context of APAP-induced liver failure.

claim: Anti-mouse Chi3l1 monoclonal antibody clone 59 (C59) had the most potent effects on inhibiting APAP-induced hepatic platelet accumulation.
source: Our data showed that clone 59 (C59) had the most potent effects on inhibiting APAP-induced hepatic platelet accumulation and attenuating AILI (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 6A comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-mChi3l1 Ab (C59) treatment.

claim: Anti-mouse Chi3l1 monoclonal antibody clone 59 (C59) had the most potent effects on attenuating AILI.
source: Our data showed that clone 59 (C59) had the most potent effects on inhibiting APAP-induced hepatic platelet accumulation and attenuating AILI (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 6B,C comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-mChi3l1 Ab (C59) treatment.

claim: rhChi3l1 was as effective as rmChi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment in Chil1-/- mice.
source: We found that rhChi3l1 was as effective as rmChi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment and increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 6D comparing PBS, rmChi3l1, and rhChi3l1 treatment.

claim: rhChi3l1 was as effective as rmChi3l1 in increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice.
source: We found that rhChi3l1 was as effective as rmChi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment and increasing AILI in Chil1-/- mice (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 6E,F comparing PBS, rmChi3l1, and rhChi3l1 treatment.

claim: The α-hChi3l1 mAb treatment could abrogate platelet recruitment in Chil1-/- mice treated with rhChi3l1.
source: To our excitement, the α-hChi3l1 mAb treatment could abrogate platelet recruitment and dramatically reduce liver injury (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 6D comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-hChi3l1 Ab treatment.

claim: The α-hChi3l1 mAb treatment could dramatically reduce liver injury in Chil1-/- mice treated with rhChi3l1.
source: To our excitement, the α-hChi3l1 mAb treatment could abrogate platelet recruitment and dramatically reduce liver injury (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by serum ALT and liver histology data shown in Figure 6E,F comparing Ctrl IgG versus α-hChi3l1 Ab treatment.

claim: mAb-based blocking of Chi3l1 may be an effective therapeutic strategy to treat AILI and potentially other acute liver injuries.
source: Together, these data indicate that mAb-based blocking of Chi3l1 may be an effective therapeutic strategy to treat AILI and potentially other acute liver injuries.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that anti-Chi3l1 antibodies can reduce platelet accumulation and liver injury.

claim: The current study unveiled an important function of Chi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment into the liver after APAP overdose.
source: The current study unveiled an important function of Chi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment into the liver after APAP overdose, thereby playing a critical role in exacerbating APAP-induced coagulopathy and liver injury.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Chi3l1 plays a critical role in exacerbating APAP-induced coagulopathy and liver injury.
source: The current study unveiled an important function of Chi3l1 in promoting platelet recruitment into the liver after APAP overdose, thereby playing a critical role in exacerbating APAP-induced coagulopathy and liver injury.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Chi3l1 promotes platelet recruitment which contributes to liver injury.

claim: Chi3l1 signals through CD44 on macrophages to upregulate podoplanin expression and promote platelet recruitment.
source: Our data demonstrate that Chi3l1 signals through CD44 on Mɸs to upregulate podoplanin expression and promote platelet recruitment (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Significant hepatic accumulation of platelets was observed in patients with ALF caused by APAP overdose.
source: Moreover, we report for the first time significant hepatic accumulation of platelets and marked upregulation of Chi3l1 in patients with ALF caused by APAP overdose.
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Marked upregulation of Chi3l1 was observed in patients with ALF caused by APAP overdose.
source: Moreover, we report for the first time significant hepatic accumulation of platelets and marked upregulation of Chi3l1 in patients with ALF caused by APAP overdose.
evidence: Supported by IHC and ELISA data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Neutralizing Chi3l1 with mAbs can effectively inhibit hepatic platelet accumulation.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that neutralizing Chi3l1 with mAbs can effectively inhibit hepatic platelet accumulation and mitigate liver injury caused by APAP, supporting the potential and feasibility of targeting Chi3l1 as a therapeutic strategy to treat AILI.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating that anti-Chi3l1 antibodies reduce platelet accumulation.

claim: Neutralizing Chi3l1 with mAbs can mitigate liver injury caused by APAP.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that neutralizing Chi3l1 with mAbs can effectively inhibit hepatic platelet accumulation and mitigate liver injury caused by APAP, supporting the potential and feasibility of targeting Chi3l1 as a therapeutic strategy to treat AILI.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating that anti-Chi3l1 antibodies reduce liver injury.

claim: The elevation of serum levels of Chi3l1 has been observed in various liver diseases.
source: The elevation of serum levels of Chi3l1 has been observed in various liver diseases (Kumagai et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2011; Nøjgaard et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2020), but studies of its involvement in liver diseases have only begun to emerge.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multiple receptors of Chi3l1 have been identified, including IL-13Rα2, CRTH2, TMEM219, and galectin-3.
source: Multiple receptors of Chi3l1 have been identified, including IL-13Rα2, CRTH2, TMEM219, and galectin-3 (Geng et al., 2018; He et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chi3l1 was upregulated during gastric cancer development and through binding to CD44, it activated Erk, Akt, and β-catenin signaling, thereby enhancing GC metastasis.
source: A recent study showed that Chi3l1 was upregulated during gastric cancer (GC) development and that through binding to CD44, it activated Erk, Akt, and β-catenin signaling, thereby enhancing GC metastasis (Geng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The role of podoplanin/Clec-2 interaction in platelet recruitment and thromboinflammation has been indicated in multiple inflammatory and infectious conditions.
source: The role of podoplanin/Clec-2 interaction in platelet recruitment and thromboinflammation has been indicated in multiple inflammatory and infectious conditions (Chauhan et al., 2020; Hitchcock et al., 2015; Kerrigan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Platelets contribute to tissue damage during injury phase but promote tissue repair at later time points.
source: An increasing number of studies suggest that platelets play an important, but paradoxical role in liver injury. It has been proposed that they contribute to tissue damage during injury phase but promote tissue repair at later time points (Chauhan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Persistent platelet accumulation in the liver significantly delays liver repair in AILI.
source: However, two recent studies of AILI demonstrate that persistent platelet accumulation in the liver significantly delays liver repair.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies mentioned in the text.

claim: AILI was associated with elevated plasma levels of von Willebrand factor, which prolonged hepatic platelet accumulation and delayed repair of APAP-injured liver in mice.
source: Another study showed that AILI was associated with elevated plasma levels of von Willebrand factor, which prolonged hepatic platelet accumulation and delayed repair of APAP-injured liver in mice (Groeneveld et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Hepatic platelet accumulation was observed as early as 3 hr after APAP treatment in mice, prior to APAP-induced liver necrosis.
source: We observed hepatic platelet accumulation as early as 3 hr after APAP treatment in mice, prior to APAP-induced liver necrosis, indicating that platelets are likely to be the driver of AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of platelet accumulation relative to liver necrosis.

claim: Platelets are likely to be the driver of AILI.
source: We observed hepatic platelet accumulation as early as 3 hr after APAP treatment in mice, prior to APAP-induced liver necrosis, indicating that platelets are likely to be the driver of AILI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that platelet accumulation occurs before liver necrosis.

claim: Mitochondrial damage is a key event in APAP-induced cell necrosis.
source: Mitochondrial damage is a key event in APAP-induced cell necrosis, in which APAP triggers c-jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation in the cytosol and translocation of phospho-JNK to the mitochondria, resulting in oxidant stress and the mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Saito et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Chi3l1 can induce phosphorylation of JNK directly in either bronchial epithelial cells or LSEC line.
source: Others and our lab have reported that Chi3l1 can induce phosphorylation of JNK directly in either bronchial epithelial cells or LSEC line (Shan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature including the authors' previous work.

claim: The Chi3l1/CD44 axis does not affect tissue recovery in AILI.
source: There were no differences in ALT levels at 72 hr post-APAP, again indicating that the Chi3l1/CD44 does not affect tissue recovery.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ALT levels at 72 hr post-APAP among WT, Chil1-/-, and Cd44-/- mice.

claim: The Chi3l1/CD44 axis is involved in the initiation and injury phases of AILI.
source: Moreover, we compared ALT levels at 6 hr post-APAP and there were lower in Chil1-/- and Cd44-/- mice than WT mice (data not shown), which were consistent with the data shown at 24 hr, indicating that Chi3l1/CD44 axis is involved in the initiation and injury phases of AILI.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ALT levels at 6 hr and 24 hr post-APAP among WT, Chil1-/-, and Cd44-/- mice.

claim: NAC is the only antidote for APAP overdose at present.
source: There is an unmet need for developing treatments for AILI, as NAC is the only antidote at present.
evidence: This is a statement about the current standard of care for APAP overdose.

claim: The efficacy of NAC declines rapidly when initiated more than a few hours after APAP overdose.
source: However, the efficacy of NAC declines rapidly when initiated more than a few hours after APAP overdose, long before patients are admitted to the clinic with symptoms of severe liver injury (Larson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: APAP overdose is the leading cause of ALF in Europe and North America.
source: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is the leading cause of ALF in Europe and North America and responsible for more cases of ALF than all other aetiologies combined (Bernal and Wendon, 2013; Jaeschke, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: More than 50 million Americans use products containing APAP each week.
source: It is estimated that each week, more than 50 million Americans use products containing APAP and approximately 30,000 patients are admitted to intensive care units every year due to APAP-induced liver injury (AILI) (Bernal and Wendon, 2013; Blieden et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Approximately 30,000 patients are admitted to intensive care units every year due to AILI.
source: It is estimated that each week, more than 50 million Americans use products containing APAP and approximately 30,000 patients are admitted to intensive care units every year due to APAP-induced liver injury (AILI) (Bernal and Wendon, 2013; Blieden et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 30% of patients with APAP overdose do not respond to NAC.
source: Although N-acetylcysteine (NAC) can prevent liver injury if given in time, there are still 30% of patients who do not respond to NAC (Fisher and Curry, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: APAP is metabolized predominantly by cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1) to a reactive toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).
source: APAP is metabolized predominantly by cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1) to a reactive toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APAP metabolism.

claim: NAPQI causes mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and eventually cell death.
source: NAPQI causes mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and eventually cell death (Hinson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The initial direct toxicity of APAP triggers the cascades of coagulation and inflammation, contributing to the progression and exacerbation of AILI.
source: The initial direct toxicity of APAP triggers the cascades of coagulation and inflammation, contributing to the progression and exacerbation of AILI (Hinson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In patients with APAP overdose, clinical observations of thrombocytopenia, reduced plasma fibrinogen levels, elevated thrombin-antithrombin, and increased levels of pro-coagulation microparticles strongly suggest concurrent coagulopathy.
source: In patients with APAP overdose, the clinical observations of thrombocytopenia, reduced plasma fibrinogen levels, elevated thrombin-antithrombin, and increased levels of pro-coagulation microparticles strongly suggest concurrent coagulopathy (Stravitz et al., 2013; Stravitz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: APAP challenge in mice causes a rapid activation of the coagulation cascade and significant deposition of fibrin(ogen) in the liver.
source: Similarly, APAP challenge in mice causes a rapid activation of the coagulation cascade and significant deposition of fibrin(ogen) in the liver (Groeneveld et al., 2020; Sullivan et al., 2012; Sullivan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In mice, APAP-induced thrombocytopenia correlates with the accumulation of platelets in the liver.
source: With regard to the role of platelets in AILI, it is reported that in mice APAP-induced thrombocytopenia correlates with the accumulation of platelets in the liver and that platelet depletion significantly attenuates AILI (Miyakawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Persistent platelet accumulation in the liver delays tissue repair after AILI in mice.
source: Two recent studies also demonstrate that persistent platelet accumulation in the liver delays tissue repair after AILI in mice (Chauhan et al., 2020; Groeneveld et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hepatic platelet accumulation is a key mechanism contributing to AILI.
source: These findings strongly indicate that hepatic platelet accumulation is a key mechanism contributing to AILI.
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies showing correlation between platelet accumulation and liver injury.

claim: Chi3l1 is a chitinase-like soluble protein without chitinase activities.
source: Chitinase 3-like-1 (Chi3l1) (YKL-40 in humans) is a chitinase-like soluble protein without chitinase activities (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Chi3l1 is produced by multiple cell types, including macrophages, neutrophils, fibroblasts, synovial cells, endothelial cells, and tumor cells.
source: It is produced by multiple cell types, including macrophages, neutrophils, fibroblasts, synovial cells, endothelial cells, and tumor cells (Hakala et al., 1993; Kawada et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chi3l1 has been implicated in multiple biological processes including apoptosis, inflammation, oxidative stress, infection, and tumor metastasis.
source: Chi3l1 has been implicated in multiple biological processes including apoptosis, inflammation, oxidative stress, infection, and tumor metastasis (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Elevated serum levels of Chi3l1 have been observed in various liver diseases, such as hepatic fibrosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver, alcoholic liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Elevated serum levels of Chi3l1 have been observed in various liver diseases, such as hepatic fibrosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver, alcoholic liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma (Kumagai et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2011; Nøjgaard et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Female mice are less susceptible to AILI than male mice.
source: Mice (8–12 weeks of age) were fasted overnight (5:00 p.m. to 9:00 a.m.) before intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected with APAP (Sigma, A7085) at a dose of 210 mg/kg for male mice and 325 mg/kg for female mice, as female mice are less susceptible to AILI (Munoz and Fearon, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and reflected in the different APAP doses used for male versus female mice.

claim: Male mice have been the choice in the vast majority of the studies of AILI reported in the literature.
source: Male mice have been the choice in the vast majority of the studies of AILI reported in the literature (Ju et al., 2002; Sullivan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The amino acid sequence homology between human and mouse Chi3l1 is 76%.
source: Because the amino acid sequence homology between human and mouse Chi3l1 is quite high (76%), we treated Chil1-/- mice with rhChi3l1.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sequence homology between human and mouse Chi3l1.
